questions.stem: In a chef's costing sheet dispute, a judge voids a rule conflicting with the master plan; what is this?

options.text: Federalism divides recipes only
Executive privilege shields the cook
Legislative supremacy overrides judges
Judicial review allows courts to invalidate conflicting laws

questions.explanation: Judicial review empowers courts to strike laws conflicting with the Constitution, keeping the legislature within bounds.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.stem: A chef's master recipe is hard to change; why does the Constitution make amendments difficult?

answer.exemplar: The amendment process requires supermajorities in Congress and among states, ensuring broad consensus and preventing hasty changes to fundamental law.

questions.explanation: High thresholds protect stability and require widespread agreement. They balance adaptability with endurance.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT

stimulus.body: Montesquieu argued liberty is safest when legislative, executive, and judicial powers are separate. Concentrating them invites tyranny.

questions.stem: In a chef's costing sheet, one station controls recipe, budget, and discipline; what risk?

options.text: Efficiency improves with faster decisions
Liberty is threatened by concentrated power
Costs always drop under one station
Morale rises under single control

questions.explanation: Concentrating powers threatens liberty by removing checks. Separation prevents any single actor from dominating.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.stem: A chef runs a loose alliance of independent kitchens; contrast with federal system.

options.text: Confederation has no central kitchen at all
Both give all power to central kitchen
Confederation keeps states supreme; federation shares sovereignty
Federation lets states ignore central rules

questions.explanation: In a confederation states remain supreme; in a federation sovereignty is shared. The Articles were confederal; the Constitution federal.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.stem: In a chef's costing sheet, the owner rejects a menu change; how can cooks enact it?

options.text: Change happens after thirty days
The rejection is permanent
One cook appeals to a judge
Override with a two-thirds vote

questions.explanation: A veto can be overridden by a two-thirds vote in both chambers, preserving legislative power against executive rejection.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.stem: A chef lists central tasks and regional leftover tasks; distinguish them.

answer.exemplar: Enumerated powers are specifically granted to the federal government, while reserved powers remain with states or the people under the Tenth Amendment.

questions.explanation: The distinction rests on explicit grants versus residual authority. Enumerated powers are finite and listed.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT

stimulus.body: Government authority derives from the consent of the governed. Elections and constitutional ratification express that consent in practice.

questions.stem: In a chef's costing sheet, who ultimately authorizes the master recipe?

options.text: The head cook by personal authority
The people through consent and elections
A foreign supplier by contract
No one; recipes arise by tradition

questions.explanation: Popular sovereignty means government authority comes from the people. Elections and ratification manifest that consent.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.stem: A chef wants the master recipe amendable yet stable; what balance does the Constitution strike?

options.text: Amendments are easy to pass for quick change
Amendments are impossible to prevent any change
Amendments require broad consensus, balancing stability and adaptability
Only the head cook may amend the recipe

questions.explanation: The amendment process demands broad consensus, keeping the Constitution stable while allowing change. It avoids both rigidity and rash revision.
